_**User (2026-09-14 19:49:56Z)**_

This branch of the project is about adding a character count to the title field. While the tests and everything were implemented, there was one edge case found from a tester. I suspect that the only way to solve this is to intercept the cancel to manually update the counter, somehow


Pulled this PR down to test it out, works good, but found one very edge case. Try editing the already created issue, delete all of the characters, then press cancel. When you press edit again, there is text in the bar, but it says the char count is 255, fixes itself once you start typing so in all I dont think this is the most necessary fix but works well.

And my response:




    Pulled this PR down to test it out, works good, but found one very edge case. Try editing the already created issue, delete all of the characters, then press cancel. When you press edit again, there is text in the bar, but it says the char count is 255, fixes itself once you start typing so in all I dont think this is the most necessary fix but works well.

Currently, the char counter is updated via an input event listener

const updateCounter = () => {
    // "maxlength" and JS string length both count UTF-16 code units, so they never disagree
    const remaining = maxLength - input.value.length;
    counter.textContent = trN(remaining, textForm1, textFormN);

    counter.classList.toggle('near-limit', remaining <= 20 && remaining > 0);
    counter.classList.toggle('at-limit', remaining <= 0);
  };
  updateCounter();
  input.addEventListener('input', updateCounter);

Essentially a lambda function that is triggered whenever input is changed.

My hypothesis is that when cancel is pressed, the value is quietly restored without updating input, and thus, not updating the counter.

Let me investigate it a bit

/**
 * The container must wrap (not be) an input with "maxlength", and supply the counter text via data attributes.
 */
export function initInputCharCounter(container: HTMLElement) {
  const input = container.querySelector<HTMLInputElement | HTMLTextAreaElement>('input[maxlength], textarea[maxlength]');
  if (!input) return;

  const maxLength = Number(input.getAttribute('maxlength'));
  const textForm1 = container.getAttribute('data-locale-chars-left-1')!;
  const textFormN = container.getAttribute('data-locale-chars-left-n')!;

  const counter = createElementFromAttrs<HTMLElement>('span', {class: 'input-char-counter'});
  container.append(counter);

  const updateCounter = () => {
    // "maxlength" and JS string length both count UTF-16 code units, so they never disagree
    const remaining = maxLength - input.value.length;
    counter.textContent = trN(remaining, textForm1, textFormN);

    counter.classList.toggle('near-limit', remaining <= 20 && remaining > 0);
    counter.classList.toggle('at-limit', remaining <= 0);
  };
  updateCounter();
  input.addEventListener('input', updateCounter);
}

export function initGlobalInput() {
  registerGlobalSelectorFunc('input, textarea', attachInputDirAuto);

  // autoFocusEnd is used for autofocus an input/textarea and move the cursor to the end of the text.
  // It is useful for "New Issue"/"New PR" pages when the title is pre-filled with prefix text (e.g.: from template or commit message)
  // The native "autofocus" isn't used because there is a delay between "focused (DOM rendering)" and "move cursor to end (our JS)", it causes flickers.
  registerGlobalInitFunc('autoFocusEnd', autoFocusEnd);
  registerGlobalInitFunc('initInputCharCounter', initInputCharCounter);
}

import {initInputCharCounter} from './common-page.ts';
import {createElementFromHTML} from '../utils/dom.ts';

function makeField(maxLength: number, value: string = ''): HTMLElement {
  const container = createElementFromHTML<HTMLElement>(`
    <div data-locale-chars-left-1="%d character left" data-locale-chars-left-n="%d characters left">
      <input maxlength="${maxLength}">
    </div>
  `);
  container.querySelector('input')!.value = value;
  initInputCharCounter(container);
  return container;
}

function counterOf(container: HTMLElement): HTMLElement {
  return container.querySelector('.input-char-counter')!;
}

describe('initInputCharCounter', () => {
  beforeEach(() => {
    document.documentElement.lang = 'en-US'; // trN resolves plural rules from the document language
  });

  test('uses the plural form for an empty field', () => {
    expect(counterOf(makeField(255)).textContent).toBe('255 characters left');
  });

  test('uses the singular form at one remaining', () => {
    expect(counterOf(makeField(255, 'x'.repeat(254))).textContent).toBe('1 character left');
  });

  test('recounts on input, which covers pasting', () => {
    const container = makeField(255);
    const input = container.querySelector('input')!;
    input.value = 'hello';
    input.dispatchEvent(new Event('input'));
    expect(counterOf(container).textContent).toBe('250 characters left');
  });

  test('is near-limit but not at-limit while characters remain', () => {
    const counter = counterOf(makeField(255, 'x'.repeat(235)));
    expect(counter.classList.contains('near-limit')).toBe(true);
    expect(counter.classList.contains('at-limit')).toBe(false);
  });

  test('is at-limit and not near-limit at zero', () => {
    const counter = counterOf(makeField(255, 'x'.repeat(255)));
    expect(counter.classList.contains('at-limit')).toBe(true);
    expect(counter.classList.contains('near-limit')).toBe(false);
  });

  test('reports a server-rendered value longer than maxlength as over', () => {
    const counter = counterOf(makeField(255, 'x'.repeat(258)));
    expect(counter.textContent).toBe('-3 characters left');
    expect(counter.classList.contains('at-limit')).toBe(true);
  });

  test('counts an astral character as two, matching maxlength', () => {
    expect(counterOf(makeField(255, '😀')).textContent).toBe('253 characters left');
  });

  test('does nothing when no input in the container has maxlength', () => {
    const container = createElementFromHTML<HTMLElement>('<div><input></div>');
    initInputCharCounter(container);
    expect(container.querySelector('.input-char-counter')).toBeNull();
  });
});

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-14 19:50:30Z)**_

Your hypothesis is right about the mechanism, but the restore isn't in cancel — it's in the **edit-show** handler:

`web_src/js/features/repo-issue.ts:387-389`
```ts
if (!issueTitleInput.value.trim()) {
  issueTitleInput.value = oldTitle;
}
```

Cancel (`:392`) only hides the form — it never touches `input.value`, so the emptied value stays in the DOM and the counter correctly reads 255. On the *next* edit-show, the pre-existing restore assigns `oldTitle` programmatically, and a programmatic `.value =` assignment does not fire an `input` event. So the text comes back and the counter doesn't. Typing one character fires `input` and it self-heals — exactly the reported symptom.

So no cancel interception is needed. One line at the restore site:

The diagnosis, so you can judge whether the fix is in the right place: cancel is not where the value gets restored. Cancel (`repo-issue.ts:393`) only toggles visibility — it never touches `input.value`, so after cancelling, the field really is empty and the counter's 255 is accurate. Programmatic `.value =` assignment doesn't fire `input`, so the counter never hears about it.

So intercepting cancel would work but would be fixing it a step early — the counter would only stay correct by coincidence, and the same staleness would return through any other path that restores the value. Dispatching at the assignment site keeps the invariant local to the code that breaks it, and matches how the codebase already handles this (`colorpicker.ts:61`, `LabelEdit.ts:54`, `repo-projects.ts:101`).

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-14 19:57:57Z)**_

It's expected behavior, and the history says so explicitly. Your dispatch-as-catchall branch is the right one.

`git log -L` on those lines lands on `5c236bd4c0` ("Fix issue/PR title edit", #30858), which rewrote the whole handler. The restore wasn't invented there — it carried over a rule from the jQuery code it replaced:

```js
if (!$editInput.val().length || $editInput.val() === $issueTitle.text()) {
  $editInput.val($issueTitle.text());   // empty → put the old title back
```

The old code applied that guard on **save**; the rewrite split it in two — the save path became `if (newTitle && newTitle !== oldTitle)` (never POSTs an empty title), and the "put the old title back" half moved to show-time, which is the line we're looking at. Same rule, two places.

So the invariant isn't "cancel restores the field." It's **"an empty title is never a valid state."** That's enforced at every layer: the client won't POST it, and the server rejects it independently (`routers/web/repo/issue.go:287-288`, `title := ctx.FormTrim("title"); if len(title) == 0`), with `binding:"Required;MaxSize(255)"` on the form struct.

That dissolves the inconsistency you spotted. Partial edits survive cancel because partially-edited text is a *valid* title — there's no revert-on-cancel contract to be inconsistent with. Empty is special because it's invalid, not because cancel is involved. Cancel genuinely does nothing but toggle visibility; the restore fires on the next *open*, which is why the counter is briefly correct in between.

Given that, changing cancel to restore the value would be a real behavior change to title editing — upstream's, not this PR's — and it would break the case where someone edits, cancels to go re-read something on the page, then reopens expecting their draft. Out of scope for a character counter.

The dispatch keeps the PR's blast radius at "the counter reflects the field," which is all it ever claimed to do. The two changes from before stand as-is; nothing committed, and `make lint-js` still needs a run.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-14 20:01:08Z)**_

Worth pushing on, so I checked the thing that would actually make it dirty.

It's not a random event — `input` is precisely the "this field's value changed" contract, and the spec's deliberate refusal to fire it on programmatic assignment is the well-known gap this idiom exists to close. The codebase already closes it the same way three times (`colorpicker.ts:61`, `LabelEdit.ts:54`, `repo-projects.ts:101`).

But the *real* objection to a synthetic dispatch isn't aesthetics, it's that it's a **broadcast**: everyone listening on that input hears it, not just your counter. So the question is who else is listening. Exactly one thing:

`common-form.ts:11` runs `applyAreYouSure('form:not(.ignore-dirty)')` over every form on the page. `#issue-title-editor` qualifies — it only gets `ignore-dirty` on successful submit (`repo-issue.ts:425`). And are-you-sure's `fieldEvents` is `'change keyup propertychange input'`, bound directly on each field (`jquery.are-you-sure.ts:187`).

So the dispatch does reach it — and that turns out to be an argument *for* it. Trace the state today, without my change:

1. Load: are-you-sure stores orig = `"hello"`.
2. You empty the field → real `input` events → form marked **dirty**.
3. Cancel → visibility toggles only → form stays **dirty**.
4. Re-open → value silently restored to `"hello"` → are-you-sure never hears → still **dirty**.

The form now matches its original value but is flagged dirty, so navigating away can raise "You have unsaved changes!" about a field you never changed. That's the same stale-listener bug as the counter, one layer over. The dispatch re-runs `checkForm`, which finds `"hello" === orig` and marks it clean.

So the broadcast isn't collateral damage here — both listeners are stale for the same reason and both want the notification. The cleaner-looking alternative (export the counter's update function and call it directly) would fix your counter and leave the dirty-flag bug in place, while coupling a generic `data-global-init` widget to one feature file.

Two honest caveats:

- I traced the are-you-sure chain through source, not in a browser. The dirty-flag half is reasoning, not an observation.
- My line uses `new Event('input')` where the other three sites use `{bubbles: true}`. are-you-sure binds directly on fields rather than delegating, so non-bubbling is sufficient and keeps the blast radius smaller — but it's a deliberate difference from the local idiom, and if you'd rather match the neighbors, `{bubbles: true}` is safe too.

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-14 20:10:44Z)**_

Right — `dispatchEvent` is called on the `<input>` itself, so the input is the event's target. Nothing "on the page" at large.

Worth being precise about the propagation, though, since it's the crux of your question. `bubbles` defaults to `false`, which skips the **bubble** phase — so the form, body, document and window never see it on the way up. But a non-bubbling event still runs the **capture** phase, window → ancestors → target. A capture-phase listener on an ancestor would fire.

I checked for that: no capture-phase `input` listener sits on an ancestor of this field. The only capture listener in the codebase that includes `'input'` is `repo-issue-pull.ts:44`, bound to the merge-box element — a sibling subtree on PR pages, not an ancestor of `#issue-title-editor`. The three `document.querySelector(...).addEventListener('input', ...)` hits are all listening on one specific unrelated element each (`#ssh-key-content`, `#org_name`, `#status_check_contexts`), not on `document`.

So the actual reach is the two listeners bound directly on that input: your `updateCounter`, and are-you-sure's `checkForm`. Both the ones from the earlier trace.

And it's worth keeping the scale in mind — this is a synthetic, synchronous event. It's effectively a direct call to those listeners wearing an event's shape. It doesn't touch the network, navigation, or anything the server or another tab could observe; the whole thing begins and ends inside that click handler.
